name: Scandinavian Defense, Modern Variation
summary: The Modern Scandinavian (B01) answers 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 with the solid queen retreat 3...Qd6, dodging tempo-hits for an easy, resilient setup.
intro: The Modern Variation of the Scandinavian Defence arises after 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qd6, in which Black recaptures with the queen and then tucks her on d6 rather than the older 3...Qa5. From d6 the queen is centralized and hard to attack profitably: she avoids the exposed a5-square, where 3...Qa5 invites Bd2, b4 and Nd5 with tempo, and she keeps an eye down the d-file at White's centre. Black then follows a simple, repeatable plan of ...Nf6, ...c6, ...e6 and ...g6 or ...Bf5, castling into a compact, low-maintenance structure. Solid and easy to handle, this treatment has become the modern main line of the Scandinavian, popular from club play all the way to the elite.
line: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The whole idea behind 3...Qd6 is safety without passivity. Compared with 3...Qa5, where the queen is repeatedly harassed by Bd2, b4 and Nd5, the d6-square gives Black a centralized queen that is difficult to hit with tempo. Black concedes a little space and a modest lead in development, and in return receives a sturdy, well-understood structure that is nearly impossible to break down with routine play. The pawns go to c6 and e6, the knights to f6 and d7, and the light-squared bishop is developed actively to f5 or g4 before ...e6 shuts it in.

White, for his part, tries to exploit the tempo spent on the queen. A broad centre with d4, quick development of Nf3, Bc4 and Bf4 or Bg5, and sometimes the lunge Nb5 or Ne5 all aim to make Black's setup uncomfortable before it is completed. Black neutralizes this by playing ...a6 early to rule out Nb5, meeting an offside knight with ...Na6 or ...Qb6 to gain time, and completing development harmoniously. Once castled, Black looks to free the position with a well-timed ...c5 or ...e5 and to trade into a comfortable, balanced middlegame.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: White's most natural continuation is 4.d4 Nf6 5.Nf3, when Black chooses between the flexible 5...a6, which rules out Nb5 and prepares ...b5, ...Bb7 or ...Bg4, and the fianchetto plan 5...g6 followed by ...Bg7 and ...O-O. A critical independent try is 5...c6 6.Ne5, when White grabs central space and Black must react precisely with ...Nbd7 and careful piece play. White can also develop actively with Bc4 together with Bf4 or Bg5, provoking the black queen, while Black answers with ...c6, ...e6 and solid piece placement.

If White lunges with an early Nb5, Black meets it calmly with ...Na6 or ...Qb6, gaining time on the offside knight before it can achieve anything. Across these lines the recurring structure is the same: Black's queen sits on d6, the pawns form a compact c6-e6 shell, and the light-squared bishop is developed before ...e6 locks it in. The play is rarely forcing, and Black relies on soundness and understanding rather than memorized tactics to reach a balanced game.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Scandinavian, once called the Centre Counter, is among the oldest recorded replies to 1.e4 and appears in the earliest chess literature. For most of its history the queen retreated to a5, but from the late twentieth century onward the centralizing 3...Qd6 — sometimes named the Gubinsky-Melts Defence after its analysts — grew into the modern main line.

Its blend of solidity and simplicity made it a practical weapon at every level. Grandmasters such as Sergei Tiviakov built long unbeaten streaks with the ...Qd6 system, and it is regularly seen from club events to elite tournaments, valued as a low-theory way for Black to reach a sound, fighting middlegame with a minimum of memorization.
